title: Placaeus: fallen man could not sin if he willed as he ought, so the power not to sin belongs to nature
source_text: XXIX. Josue Placaeus vero videtur aliquid amplius dicere, sed tamen quod eodem redit, quantum ad summam rei. Docet enim, quantacunque sit hominis corruptio, illum posse non peccare si vellet, & si ad non peccandum voluntas ejus esset, uti decet, comparata. Adeoque facultatem non peccandi in homine, si istud serio velit & ut oportet, non ascribendam esse gratiae, sed naturae. Affirmat enim eam facultatem etiam homini corrupto inesse, ut non modo peccare possit si velit, sed etiam non peccare, si quidem, uti par est, a peccato voluntas ejus abhorreret. Quare, inquit, non bene considerasse rerum naturas videntur illi qui facultatem non peccandi, si ad non peccandum, uti decet, comparata esset voluntas, gratiae tribuunt, cum sit potius ascribenda naturae, qua fit ut involuntarii & peccati rationes inter se pugnent. Unde colligit frustra nobis objici ea scripturae loca, quibus tribuit eam facultatem homini, ut possit bene agere si velit: nempe quomodo eum decet velle. Tractatu de libero arbitrio cap. 4.
pass_a_gloss: XXIX. But Josué de la Place seems to say something more, but yet what comes to the same thing, as to the sum of the matter. For he teaches that, however great the corruption of man may be, he could not sin if he willed, and if his will were disposed for not sinning, as is fitting. And so that the faculty of not sinning in man, if he wills it seriously and as he ought, is to be ascribed not to grace, but to nature. For he affirms that faculty to be in man even corrupt, so that not only can he sin if he will, but also not sin, if indeed, as is right, his will shrank from sin. Wherefore, he says, those seem not to have considered well the natures of things who attribute to grace the faculty of not sinning, if the will were disposed for not sinning as is fitting, since it is rather to be ascribed to nature, by which it comes about that the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other. Whence he gathers that those places of scripture are objected to us in vain, which attribute that faculty to man, that he can act well if he will: namely in the way it befits him to will. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.
pass_b_english: Josué de la Place seems to go further, though in substance he arrives at the same place. However deep man's corruption, he teaches, man could avoid sin if he willed to, that is, if his will were set against sinning as it ought to be. So the ability not to sin, given a serious and proper willing, is to be credited to nature and not to grace.

He holds that even corrupt man has this ability: he can sin if he wishes, and he can also not sin, provided his will recoils from sin as it should. 'So,' he says, 'those who credit grace with the ability not to sin, on the condition that the will were rightly set against sinning, seem not to have weighed the nature of things well. It belongs rather to nature, which makes the notions of the involuntary and of sin conflict with each other.'
From this he concludes that it is useless to cite against us the scriptures that grant man the ability to do good if he wills, meaning if he wills as he should. Treatise on free choice, chapter 4.
